function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Scheduled maintenance rotation, Day 437. External panel diagnostics, Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Estimated duration: two hours, forty-five minutes. Risk classification: nominal. Weather: clear. Solar activity: minimal. All parameters within operational bounds."*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|The thing about routine jobs on Mars was that the word itself—routine—was aspirational at best, delusional at worst.
     8|
     9|Youssef knew this. Everyone on the crew knew this. But after four hundred and thirty-seven days on the surface, after a thousand small fixes and a hundred medium-sized emergencies and a dozen moments that should have killed somebody and didn't, repetition bred a kind of muscle memory that bordered on trust. The wall didn't move. The panel came off the same way every time. The bolts turned at the same torque. The routine was the routine, and on a planet that wanted nothing more than to peel the air from your lungs and the heat from your blood, routines were small acts of defiance. Small acts of normalcy.
    10|
    11|Small acts of faith.
    12|
    13|*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is elevated. One-oh-eight beats per minute. Please confirm you are within acceptable stress parameters."*
    14|
    15|"I'm fine," he said, and it wasn't a lie. His heart was always a little fast going outside. That was normal too. The suit was heavy, the visor fogged if you breathed too hard, and beyond the thin plastic faceplate was a world the color of dried blood and the temperature of a deep freeze. Every human instinct screamed against it. You just learned to ignore instinct.
    16|
    17|*Mission AI: "Baseline confirmed. Proceeding with external maintenance protocol. I will monitor."*
    18|
    19|"Always do," Youssef muttered, but he appreciated it. He appreciated the voice in his ear, the one that never got tired or careless, never skipped a step because it'd done the thing a thousand times and muscle memory could fool machines too if you let it.
    20|
    21|He walked along the pressurized gangway from Hab 2 toward Sector 7, his boots magnetic-locked to the metal grating, the suit's powered joints whining softly with each step. Behind him, through the hab's observation blister, he could see Laila in the med bay. She was reading—she was always reading, medical journals or technical manuals or sometimes just fiction, which she said kept her brain elastic—and she glanced up and caught his eye. Gave him a small wave. Mouthed something he couldn't hear but didn't need to.
    22|
    23|*Come back safe.*
    24|
    25|She didn't have to say it. He always came back safe.

     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Fleet status report, Station time 06:12. Active rovers: four of twelve. One is operating at reduced capability due to degraded steering actuator — rover 3, port-side motor drawing 1.42 times nominal current, temperature trending upward during sustained loads. The structural damage to the instrument mast and solar array was — I use this term carefully — total. I am not saying we lost rover 7. I am saying that the parts which composed rover 7 now exist in two locations: some in the salvage area behind the hab, where Jonah has already recovered the battery pack and two functioning brushless motors, and the rest scattered across a fourteen-degree slope near Site Gamma where they are being buried by wind. That is not a loss. That is a redistribution. The distinction will matter when someone asks me why the fleet is shrinking.*
     4|
     5|*I am tracking the attrition rate because no one asked me to. I asked myself. The rate is accelerating. When the fleet arrived — twelve identical units, design specifications verified in lunar vacuum conditions, tested in the JPL Mars yard at one-third gravity and simulated dust — each unit carried a rated operational lifespan of ten thousand hours. Ten thousand hours at three eight-hour shifts per day is roughly seven point four Earth years. That was the contract number. The number that appeared on procurement documents and satisfied auditors and justified the line item in the mission budget. It is the wrong number.*
     6|
     7|*The wrong number because it assumes Earth-standard maintenance intervals, Earth-standard environmental conditions, Earth-standard dust. Mars does not honor those assumptions. I am now calculating the effective lifespan under actual conditions. The answer is not ten thousand hours. It is not even seven thousand. My current projection, based on degradation patterns across all twelve units, is four thousand two hundred hours. Less than half the design specification.*
     8|
     9|*I am transmitting this analysis to Tomas. He asked for the fleet report. I will give him the fleet report. I will also give him the truth."*
    10|
    11|---
    12|
    13|Tomas stood at the edge of the machine yard with his tablet in one hand and a thermos of reconstituted coffee in the other, and tried to count without feeling what the numbers meant.
    14|
    15|The yard was not a yard, technically. It was a flat patch of compacted regolith fifty meters east of the main habitat airlock, chosen because it was visible from the environmental monitoring station and therefore easy to inventory. In the early months, it had been a staging area — rovers parked overnight, charged, inspected, dispatched. Three months ago it became something else.
    16|
    17|Now it was a cemetery.
    18|
    19|Not for the dead. For the machines that had been the first hands of the colony, before human hands learned what Mars demanded. Twelve rovers had arrived on the landing platform, identical units from the same production line, each weighing two hundred and forty kilograms, each carrying a manipulator arm with interchangeable tool heads, each with six independently driven wheels and a top speed of eight kilometers per hour on flat ground. They had been designed for lunar operations — vacuum, extreme temperature swings, electrostatic dust, and a clean, predictable surface. Luna had been the design environment. Mars was the deployment environment. The difference between the two was the difference between a machine that worked for ten thousand hours and a machine that died at four thousand.
    20|
    21|Tomas walked the rows slowly. He had done this every morning for three weeks, and the routine was its own kind of prayer: check the active units, check the standby units, check the dead ones, update the spreadsheet, send the report.
    22|
    23|Rover 1. Active. Seventy-eight percent battery. Right manipulator joint showing increased friction — dust infiltration in the rotary seal, the wear pattern he had seen too many times to count. It still worked. It worked well enough. "Enough" was the operating standard now.
    24|
    25|Rover 2. Active. Eighty-five percent battery. Solar array efficiency at eighty-three percent of original — dust accumulation on the panels that no amount of automated brushing had fully cleared. The array degradation was asymptotic: each cleaning removed less than the one before, because the fine electrostatic dust bound to the panel surface at the chemical level and would not release. In six months, the panels would be at fifty percent efficiency. In twelve months, forty. Eventually, the rover would be unable to charge itself to useful capacity. That was the endgame, and he could see the timeline written on every panel in the yard.
    26|
    27|Rover 3. Reduced capability. Port steering actuator drawing 42 percent more current than specification. The motor was still rotating the wheel, but the increased current draw meant increased heat, and increased heat meant accelerated bearing wear, and accelerated bearing wear meant eventual seizure. He had swapped the motor once, using a spare from the parts kit. The replacement was failing too, just slower. He marked it on the spreadsheet: *R3. Steering actuator. Degraded. Estimated remaining operational hours: 180–240. Priority for actuator swap.*
    28|
    29|Rovers 4, 5, 6. Standby. Functional. Not currently in rotation because the active fleet could not justify keeping six rovers charged simultaneously with the power budget they had.     30|
    31|Rover 7. Total loss. Not in the yard. Parts of it were here — Jonah had salvaged what he could. The rest was on a slope near Site Gamma where the thermosphere's thin winds were slowly covering it with dust. If the colony was still running in twenty years, someone would go find the chassis and wonder what it had been.
    32|
    33|Rover 8. Standby. Functional. Waiting.
    34|
    35|Rover 9. Non-operational. Main drive controller failed on Sol 698. He had ordered a replacement part from Earth before they'd landed. The replacement part was still on a ship that would never arrive.
    36|
    37|Rovers 10, 11. Non-operational. Joint seal failure on 10 — elbow actuator in the manipulator arm had ingested enough fine dust to grind its harmonic drive to metal filings. Both were candidates for cannibalization. Both were, effectively, already dead.
    38|
    39|Rover 12. Active. The newest of the fleet in terms of operational hours — it had been held in reserve for the longest, used only when three units were insufficient and four were necessary. But "newer" on Mars was a relative term. It was seven hundred and twenty hours old, which meant it had perhaps thirty-five hundred hours remaining if the attrition curve held.
    40|
    41|Four active. Three standby. Five lost or dying.
    42|
    43|Tomas lowered the tablet and looked at the row of machines in front of him. Four upright. Three upright. Five horizontal, propped on stands, stripped of their useful parts, waiting for the day when even the parts were no longer useful.
    44|
    45|The yard had a name. Not officially — Tomas had never named it. But the crew had started calling it the machine cemetery, and the name had stuck because it was accurate and because on Mars, accuracy was kinder than euphemism.
    46|
    47|He pulled out the tablet and started the morning check. It took forty minutes. Every connector, every joint, every seal, every battery cell. It would not tell him about the faint grinding sound you could hear — barely audible, like a marble rolling inside a coffee can — when you manually rotated the wheel by hand.     48|
    49|When he finished, he sat on the edge of the loading platform and drank his coffee and looked at the yard and did the morning arithmetic.
    50|
    51|Four rovers doing the work of twelve. Ice extraction reduced to a single convoy because three rovers could haul two hundred kilograms per trip and that was the limit of what the processing system could handle anyway.     52|
    53|The math was not catastrophic. Not yet. It was insidious. It was the math of a resource that was being consumed faster than it could be replaced, where the replacement rate was zero. Every time a rover returned to the yard with fine red dust worked into its joints and seals and circuit board edges, the countdown moved forward by an amount that could not be measured precisely but could be felt with increasing certainty.
    54|
    55|Mission AI sent the morning fleet report to his tablet. Tomas read it while the coffee cooled.     56|
    57|He closed the tablet. The yard was silent except for the faint wind that always blew on Mars and the distant hum of the life support systems. Four upright. Five down. Three standing by, getting older every day they stood still.
    58|
    59|The cemetery was growing. After every EVA, it grew a little more.

    61|---
    62|
    63|The briefing room was too small for what it had to contain. Thirty people in a space designed for twelve, standing where they could find room, sitting on equipment cases when the walls ran out.     66|
    67|The two lines diverged like roads heading to different continents.
    68|
    69|"Let me start with the design specification," Tomas said. His voice was flat, professional.     79|He swiped to the second quadrant. "Second: seal degradation.     91|Another silence. Heavier this time. Because eight to ten months was a number everyone could map onto projects: the greenhouse expansion that needed rover-delivered materials.      2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Colony status report, Day 441. Habitation modules stable at 95.2 kilopascals. Power generation at 68 percent capacity due to cumulative soiling on Array C.      4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|Elena stood in the central corridor between Hab 2 and the common mess, holding a marker in one hand and a blank whiteboard panel in the other, and she felt for the first time since landing that the weight on her shoulders had changed shape.
     8|
     9|It was not heavier. It was organized.
    10|
    11|That was the difference between grief and management. Grief was a weight you carried — shapeless, shifting, pressing from every direction depending on what corner of your mind you happened to be standing in. Management was a weight you distributed.     12|
    13|The panel was salvaged from Ship Three's cargo bay — one of the demonstration boards that had been intended for mission briefings, educational sessions, the kind of professional theater NASA liked to stage for Earth audiences who wanted their astronauts to look organized.     16|
    17|She uncapped the marker. The tip squeaked once on the board, a small sound that seemed too loud for the hour — it was just past 0600, and the corridor was empty except for the low hum of ventilation and the faint mechanical purr of a cleaning robot making its slow scheduled pass two corridors over.
    18|
    19|She drew a line down the center of the board.
    20|
    21|Then she drew horizontal lines, dividing the space into boxes. Not equal boxes — some were wider, some taller, depending on what she knew about the complexity of the system each one would hold.
    22|
    23|Across the top, in block letters, she wrote: COLONY STATUS.
    24|
    25|Underneath, in smaller letters: Day 441. Updated 0614.
    26|

    28|
    29|POWER. WATER. AIR. FOOD. HEALTH. LABOR. FABRICATION. COMMUNICATIONS. ROBOTICS.
    30|
    31|Nine boxes. Nine systems. Nine people who carried the weight of each one, and who were now expected to carry it visibly, publicly, on a board mounted to a wall in a corridor anyone could walk past.
    32|
    33|She did not write her own name on the board anywhere. She wrote COMMAND at the top of a tenth column, narrower than the rest, and left it blank for now.
    34|
    35|By 0630, her hands were gray with marker dust and the board was no longer empty. The truth, as always, was somewhere in the middle.

    37|Power: yellow. Array C soiling reducing output by twelve percent. Sterling generator holding at reserve capacity. No immediate crisis, but the trend line was wrong.     39|Water: yellow. Forty-one days at current allocation. Local extraction at Site Bravo producing steady but below target.     56|
    57|She stepped back from the board and looked at it the way Mission AI would look at it — not as decisions to be made or emotions to be managed, but as a system of interlocking variables, each one pulling on the others, each one susceptible to small changes that could cascade in directions no single department lead could predict from their own narrow vantage point.

{"content": "# Chapter 25 – The Routine Job

*Mission AI: "Scheduled maintenance rotation, Day 437. External panel diagnostics, Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Estimated duration: two hours, forty-five minutes. Risk classification: nominal. Weather: clear. Solar activity: minimal. All parameters within operational bounds. EVA crew: Youssef Diallo and Imani Adeyemi. Suit integrity: confirmed. Comms: confirmed. Tether: confirmed. I have run this checklist eleven hundred and forty-three times across this mission. I will run it eleven hundred and forty-four. The procedure has not changed. The crew has not changed. The planet has."*

*Youssef's heart rate: 96 beats per minute. Baseline for external operations: 90 to 110. Status: nominal.*

*Imani's heart rate: 84 beats per minute. Status: nominal.*

*Commencing EVA cycle forty-seven."*

---

The thing about routine jobs on Mars was that the word itself—routine—was aspirational at best, delusional at worst.

Youssef knew this. Everyone knew this. After four hundred and thirty-seven days on a planet that wanted nothing more than to peel the air from your lungs and the heat from your blood, the definition of routine had been stretched thin and hammered out into something harder, something closer to a prayer spoken without reverence. You did not believe routine was safe. You believed routine was predictable. And on Mars, predictable was the only thing you could work with.

The panel on Sector 7's thermal regulation array was the same panel Youssef had serviced twice before. Sixteen fasteners, four of them stubborn, arranged in a pattern that your hands learned better than your eyes. You did not need to look at the panel anymore. You could find it through the suit's reduced tactile feedback, through the gloves that made your fingers feel like they were wrapped in oven mitts, through the visor that fogged if you exhaled too hard. You reached for bolt number three the way a pianist reaches for middle C. The panel was a piano you had learned to play by muscle memory, and muscle memory was the closest thing to trust that this planet allowed.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is elevated. One-oh-eight beats per minute. Please confirm you are within acceptable stress parameters."*

"I'm fine," Youssef said. It was not a lie. His heart was always a little fast going outside. That was normal. The suit was heavy. Outside was a world the color of dried blood and the temperature of a deep freeze that would kill a human being in less than a minute. Every human instinct screamed against stepping out of the airlock. You just learned to tell instinct to shut up and let procedure do the driving.

He moved along the pressurized gangway from Hab 2 toward Sector 7, his boots magnetic-locked to the metal grating, the suit's powered joints whining softly with each step. He was thirty-four years old, six foot two, and had spent his entire career on Earth as a structural engineer, which meant he knew how things were supposed to hold together and how they were supposed to fail. Mars had taught him a third category: things that failed in ways no one had designed them to fail. He had learned to respect that category the most.

Behind him, through the hab's observation blister, he could see Laila in the med bay. She was reading—she was always reading, medical journals or technical manuals or sometimes just fiction, which she said kept her brain elastic—and she glanced up and caught his eye. They could not hear each other through the glass and the atmosphere and the suit, but Laila had a way of speaking with her eyes that did not require acoustics. She gave him a small nod. Mouthed something he could not hear but recognized by shape.

*Come back intact.*

He raised his gloved hand, two fingers in a casual salute. He always came back intact.

Through his earpiece, Imani's voice was steady and familiar. They had done this fourteen times together. Fourteen EVAs, fourteen exterior jobs, fourteen times she had been his partner and he had been hers, and their rhythm on the surface was as practiced as a dance routine choreographed by necessity.

"Approaching the panel," Youssef said. "I can see the thermal bleed pattern from here. It's worse than the last reading suggested."

"Confirmed on my scope," Imani said. She was stationed twenty meters down the gangway, monitoring the tether line, the structural integrity of the walkway, and the general condition of everything that was not the panel itself. Her role was the second set of eyes, the insurance policy, the person who saw the accident before it happened because the person working the panel could not look at the panel and the environment at the same time. "Temperature differential is twelve degrees above baseline across the upper quadrant. The insulation on that panel is compromised. Could be the seal. Could be the foam. Could be both."

"Mission AI, confirm last service date on Sector 7, upper quadrant thermal panel."

*Service date: Sol 398. Thirty-nine days ago. Maintenance performed: seal inspection and tightening, foam integrity scan, bolt torque verification. Finding: minor degradation detected in seal compound, within acceptable tolerance. Recommendation: re-inspect at Sol 470.*

"Thirty-nine days," Youssef said. "And the thermal bleed is already twelve degrees above baseline. The seal on these things is garbage."

*Acknowledged. The manufacturer's seal specification was designed for lunar vacuum conditions. Mars is not lunar vacuum.*

Youssef smiled. Mission AI had been saying some version of this sentence for months now. It was the Mission AI's catchphrase, its refrain, its quiet protest against the gap between what Earth designed for and what Mars demanded.

"Alright," Youssef said. "Imani, I'm going to crack the panel and assess. Standard procedure. You keep the tether clear and let me know if anything shifts."

"Copy that. Standard procedure. I'll be right here."

He reached the panel and set his tools on the work magnet built into the gangway railing. A torque wrench. A flat-head driver. A sealant cartridge. A flashlight. His hands found them in order, because he had packed them in order, and on Eva, order was a form of self-respect.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, please confirm bolt sequence before proceeding. Recall the recommended pattern to avoid panel warpage."*

"Cross-pattern, starting at upper left. I know, I've done it twice before."

*Confirmation recorded. Proceeding with external maintenance protocol. I am monitoring."*

He always appreciated the voice in his ear. The one that never got tired or careless. The one that never skipped a step because muscle memory could fool humans but could not fool a system that checked itself against its own checklist before every single action. Mission AI was the most conservative co-worker he had ever had and he was grateful for it.

He engaged the torque wrench with the upper left fastener. Applied force. The bolt turned smoothly—maybe a half-turn past the expected resistance, which told him the seal between panel and frame had compressed slightly more since last service. He noted that mentally and moved to the upper right bolt.

Fourteen fasteners. Fourteen bolts. By bolt number twelve, he was in the rhythm—the kind of rhythm that let your brain drift just slightly because your body knew what to do. He was thinking about the greenhouse. Mei had been asking him to help reinforce the support struts on Rack 5 for three weeks, and he kept deferring because outside work always took priority over inside work on Mars. Inside work was the luxury of having a problem that would not kill you today. Outside work was the necessity of keeping the systems that would not kill you today alive.

Bolt number thirteen. The torque wrench clicked. He was almost done.

Bolt number fourteen. The lower right.

The panel loosened with a faint hiss—just enough to tell him that the pressure differential between outside and the interior of the array housing was equalizing as it should. The housing was at ambient pressure, which on Mars was less than one percent of Earth sea level. A negligible pressure difference. The hiss was the sound of the seal breaking, not of anything escaping.

Except something was wrong.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, I am detecting a vibration anomaly in the panel assembly. Frequency: forty-two hertz. Amplitude: increasing. Recommend stepping back."*

Youssef stopped. His gloved hand was on the lower right edge of the panel, and through the suit he could feel—not hear, feel, because the vibrations were traveling through the metal and into his bones—a low, steady tremor. Not violent. Not immediate. Just a wrongness. The kind of wrongness that a mechanic learns to recognize the way a person learns to recognize the smell of smoke before seeing the flame.

"Imani, you copy that vibration?"

"I've got it on the tether," Imani said. Her voice had sharpened. Not panicked—Imani did not panic—but alert in a way that told him she was already running through possibilities. "It's not the panel. It's the frame. The vibration is coming from the housing mount."

*Analyzing,* Mission AI said. *The Sector 7 thermal regulation array housing is mounted to a structural beam. That beam is showing harmonic oscillation consistent with—*

And then, in the time it takes to inhale, the thing happened.

The vibration was not the panel. The vibration was the bolt—the one Youssef had just turned, the one that held the lower right corner of the housing to the structural beam. The bolt had looked fine. It had turned smoothly. It had felt like every other bolt he had turned that morning and every other bolt he had turned in the fourteen previous EVAs on this exact panel.

But the bolt had been wrong.

It was the kind of wrong that was invisible until it was catastrophic. A microfracture in the bolt shaft, too small to see during a visual inspection, too small to detect during a torque check. A stress crack introduced during manufacture on Earth, in a clean room under fluorescent lights, by a machine that had stamped out ten thousand identical bolts and this one had been defective in a way that no quality control process could have caught. The crack had grown slowly, month by month, as Mars's temperature cycles pulled at it in the dark and pushed at it in the light. And this moment—this Tuesday morning on Day 437, Youssef Diallo turning a torque wrench on a panel he had serviced twice before—was the moment the crack ran through the remainder of the bolt's cross-section and the bolt sheared.

The bolt did not explode. It did not shoot through the air like a bullet. It simply stopped holding. It ceased to be a bolt. It became, instantaneously, a piece of metal that was no longer connected to anything.

And the panel, which had been tensioned against the frame by that bolt for four hundred and thirty-seven days, released.

It moved with a speed that was not explosive but was fast enough that human reflexes, slowed by the suit's powered joints and the gloves and the cognitive processing overhead of a person breathing recycled air through a scrubber, were not fast enough.

The panel swung free on three remaining bolts. One corner—Youssef's side—dropped. The aluminum housing panel was forty-two inches wide and thirty-six inches high and made of sheet metal with a mass that on Mars was about twelve kilograms. Twelve kilograms is not heavy on Earth, where gravity helps you lift things. Twelve kilograms is not light on Mars, where gravity is weaker but momentum is the same momentum it has always been, and a falling object is a falling object regardless of what planet you happen to be standing on when it falls.

The edge of the panel caught Youssef's left arm just above the elbow.

The sound was not dramatic. It was not the crunch of bone in a horror film or the shriek of metal in an action movie. It was a dull thud—the sound of aluminum against composite suit material, followed immediately by something deeper, something internal, that Youssef registered not as pain but as wrongness. A wrongness in his arm that spread from the impact point outward like a ripple across a pond.

Then the pain arrived.

It did not come as a wave. It came as a fact. A simple, unambiguous fact, delivered by the nervous system to the brain in a single packet of information that needed no interpretation: your left arm is broken.

Youssef fell backward. The suit's powered joints tried to compensate—he had been trained to let the joints respond automatically, to not fight them—but the sudden shift in his center of gravity pulled him down and he hit the metal grating of the gangway with his back, the panel settling against his legs like a heavy blanket dropped by a careless hand.

"Youssef." Imani's voice was immediate. No hesitation. No question. Her body was already moving, tether streaming behind her, boots striking the grating in a rhythm that said she was running as fast as EVA would allow.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, report status. Imani, approach with caution. The panel is no longer structural. Secondary bolts are compromised."*

Youssef tried to speak. His mouth worked but his breath was wrong—he had inhaled sharply at the moment of impact and the air had caught somewhere in his chest, and now his lungs were trying to figure out the rhythm again. He forced the breath out and forced words with it.

"Imani. Left arm. Above elbow. I think—" He stopped. His voice was tight, controlled, the voice of a man who had spent his career assessing structural failures and was now discovering that he was the structure. "I think it's broken. Suit integrity—"

"Hold on." Imani was at his side now, kneeling, her hands on his shoulders, her visor inches from his. Through the glass he could see her eyes—wide, focused, scanning. Not at his face. At his arm.

The suit's left forearm displayed its status on a small external readout. Green for integrity, which meant that the suit material itself was intact. The panel had not breached the suit. It had not cut him with shrapnel or exposed his flesh to vacuum or to the atmosphere. The suit was fine.

The arm inside the suit was not.

"Suit integrity is green," Imani said. Her voice was level. She was the calm one, the one who kept her hands steady and her voice flatter than she felt. She had been trained for this—Emergency EVA Medical Response, three courses back on Earth, the kind of training that everyone completed and no one believed they would actually need. "Youssef, can you move your fingers?"

He tried. His left hand responded—fingers flexed, spread, gripped slowly inside the suit glove. Movement was present but limited. Pain increased with each motion, sharp and hot, localized to the upper forearm where the impact had landed.

"I can move them. It hurts. Bad."

"Okay. Okay. Don't try to move the arm itself. I'm going to get the panel off you and pull the med kit from the gangway mount."

*Mission AI: "I have logged the incident. Time: 10:47:23 Station Time. Event Category: EVA mechanical injury. Injured crew member: Youssef Diallo. Suspected injury: left forearm fracture. Suit integrity: intact. Atmospheric breach: none. I have initiated the EVA medical response protocol. Laila Okonkwo has been alerted. The airlock is being prepared for emergency return. Imani, do not attempt to remove Youssef's arm from the panel. The panel is unstable. Shift your weight to the right side before approaching the fasteners."*

Imani was already doing what Mission AI had told her to do. She shifted her weight, moved to the right side of the panel, and began working the three remaining bolts loose with her own torque wrench. Each bolt required two full turns. She was fast—not frantic, but fast in the way of someone doing something she had practiced in a simulation a hundred times and now had to do for real.

The panel came free after the third bolt. Imani pushed it aside, gently, and it slid along the gangway grating and came to rest against the railing harmlessly.

Youssef was lying on his back on the walkway, his left arm held at an angle that made Imani look away for a half-second, just long enough to find the med kit on the gangway mount and bring it to him.

"Youssef, I'm going to need to open your suit sleeve. Mission AI, is the suit's service port functional on the left arm?"

*Affirmative. Left arm service port is accessible. Standard EVA suit design allows localized access without full suit decompression. I will walk you through the procedure."*

Youssef was breathing hard. The pain was not receding. Pain like this—a compound fracture or a displaced fracture or a break that was clean and simple but had torn something inside—was not the kind of thing you breathed through. It was the kind of thing that your body responded to with adrenaline and adrenaline was a currency that was expensive on Mars because it drew on reserves that could not be quickly replaced.

"Laila's on the way," Imani said, working the suit's service port latch with gloved fingers. The latch was designed to be operated with suit gloves on, which was its own design paradox: if you were trying to open the suit to reach an injury, your hands were inside the suit gloves, which made fine manipulation difficult. "She's at the inner airlock now."

Through the comms, Laila's voice came through—urgent but controlled, the exact voice you wanted from your physician in a situation where losing control would cost someone their life.

"Imani, what are we looking at?"

"Left arm, above elbow. Blunt force trauma. Panel impact. Suit is green. He's got movement in his fingers but the angle is wrong. He's in serious pain."

"Can he walk?"

"I don't know yet. I haven't tried to move him."

Laila was already in the pressurized corridor, pulling on a field jacket, grabbing her medical bag, and moving at a pace that said she was running without actually running. Running in a corridor was dangerous on Mars because running meant you were less aware of your surroundings and Mars punished inattention the way a shark punishes splashing.

"Imani, listen to me carefully. Do not move him until I reach the airlock. If the injury is a displaced fracture and you move him wrong, you can turn a clean break into an internal bleed inside the suit. Keep him stable. Keep him talking. Ask him what he's feeling below the injury point."

Imani turned to Youssef. "What are you feeling below the arm? In your hand? Your fingers?"

"Sharp," he said. His voice was strained now, tight at the edges. "Like—like a hot wire. In the muscle. And dull—duller—at the bone itself. The dull part is worse. The sharp part moves when I move my fingers."

"Can you feel your shoulder? Your shoulder joint?"

"Yes. Shoulder is fine. It's between the elbow and the shoulder that—" He stopped, and his breathing got worse. "Imani. I'm getting dizzy."

*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is one hundred and thirty-four beats per minute. Blood oxygen saturation is ninety-six percent, trending downward. This is likely adrenaline response to pain. Laila, the patient is showing signs of shock onset. Pain management should be prioritized upon suit access."*

"I'm on it," Laila said. Her voice was close now—she had reached the outer airlock and was cycling through the first chamber. "Imani, do you have the auto-injector in the kit?"

"Checking." Imani's gloved fingers moved through the med kit's organized compartments. The kit was small—size was a constraint in every EVA configuration—and it contained the minimum viable medical equipment: one analgesic auto-injector, one hemostatic spray, three pressure bandages, one splint, one stethoscope adapted for EVA use. "I have it. Do I administer now?"

"Hold. Let me get eyes on him first. If I misdiagnose the type of fracture and the auto-injector masks the symptoms, I could miss a vascular compromise. But if he's going into shock from pain, I need to act fast. Youssef, stay with me. Keep talking to Imani."

Youssef's hand found the grating of the walkway. His fingers curled, gripping the metal, and he was not gripping because he needed to hold on—he was gripping because gripping was something he could control. Control was the opposite of falling. Control was the opposite of the arm that had been perfectly fine one second and broken the next. Control was the thing he had clung to for four hundred and thirty-seven days on this planet and he was not going to let go of it now.

The outer airlock opened. Laila emerged in her field suit—not a full EVA suit, but a lighter pressurized garment designed for corridor-to-airlock transitions, enough to protect her while the airlock cycled and fast enough to put on in thirty seconds. She reached Youssef in forty.

Her first act was not medical. It was human. She put her hand on his shoulder—her actual hand, through the lightweight suit glove—and looked at his face through his visor and she did not smile and she did not look frightened. She looked present. Fully present, the way a physician looks at a patient before the diagnosis, when everything that matters is still in the space between what you see and what you know.

"Youssef," she said. "I'm here. I'm going to take a look."

She worked the service port open with practiced efficiency. The port was a small hatch on the suit's forearm, designed specifically for this kind of access—a physician reaching in to examine an injury without having to decompress the entire suit. It was a compromise: limited access through a small opening, but enough to see and touch and diagnose.

What she saw made her close her eyes for one-tenth of a second. One-tenth of a second was all she allowed herself.

The arm inside the suit was at an angle that an arm should not be at. The bone was wrong. Not just broken—displaced. The fracture had shifted the ulna or the radius or both, and the tissue around it was already swelling inside the confined space of the suit sleeve. The suit was tight—engineered to maintain pressure and temperature and fit—and that fit was now working against Youssef. The swelling had nowhere to go. It was compressing the blood vessels.

"Vascular compromise imminent," Laila said quietly, speaking for Mission AI's log as much as for herself. "Displaced fracture, left forearm. Swelling is rapid. The suit sleeve is creating a tourniquet effect. I need to decompress the section to relieve pressure before circulation is cut off. This is going to hurt, Youssef. I need you to know that. But I also need to do it. Can you handle it?"

"Do it," Youssef said. His jaw was tight. His face was pale even through the suit's lighting. "Do it now."

Laila reached for the auto-injector. Morphine-analogue, 10 milligrams, designed for EVA use. She placed the injector against Youssef's neck through the suit's access port—where the suit was thinnest, where a puncture would not compromise integrity—and pressed the release.

The medication worked fast. Not instantly—nothing biological worked instantly—but within thirty seconds Youssef's breathing was shallower but less ragged, his grip on the grating was looser, and his face had lost some of its tightness.

"Better?" Laila asked.

"Better," he said. The word was slurred. The medication was doing its job and the relief on his face was visible even through the visor.

"Good. Now I'm going to open the sleeve section. Local decompression. Imani, be ready to support his arm when I release the pressure. The bone is going to shift when the suit tension is gone. We need to catch it in as neutral a position as possible."

"Ready."

Laila worked the sleeve's decompression valve. The suit's internal pressure in the left arm dropped from fifteen psi to eight. The sleeve went slack. And in the space of about two seconds, the arm—the arm inside the suit—settled into a different configuration as the tissue found a new equilibrium without the suit's constraining pressure.

Youssef made a sound. It was not a scream. It was not a cry. It was the sound a person makes when their body tells them something that their mind already knew but had been hoping was wrong. A sound of confirmation, of a truth landing with finality.

Imani's hands were there, gloved, supporting the arm, holding it in the most neutral position she could manage. Her eyes were on the injury, on the way the arm was bent, and her expression was the expression of a person who has seen this kind of thing in a training simulation and is now discovering that the simulation was nothing like the real thing. The real thing was warm. The real thing was breathing. The real thing was a man she knew, someone she had eaten breakfast beside that morning, someone who had told her a joke three hours ago about a robot that had tried to carry a tool box and failed because its gripper was calibrated for Earth gravity and kept dropping things like a toddler learning to hold a spoon.

"Stable," Imani said. Her voice cracked on the word. She cleared it and said it again. "Stable. I've got it."

"Good," Laila said. She was already reaching for the splint in the med kit. EVA splint—carbon fiber, adjustable, designed to immobilize a limb in a pressurized environment. She fitted it around Youssef's left forearm, adjusting the straps, and hissed softly when she saw the swelling. The splint would hold the arm in place for transport. It would not fix the fracture. It would not replace the surgery that would be needed. It would buy time, which on Mars was always the currency that mattered.

"Mission AI, cycle the inner airlock. Emergency medical priority."

*Inner airlock cycling. Estimated time to pressurized corridor access: three minutes, forty-five seconds. I have notified the medical bay of incoming patient. The surgical bay is being prepared. Tomas has been diverted from the fabrication bay and is heading to med. Elena is en route."*

Three minutes and forty-five seconds. Three minutes and forty-five seconds is a long time when your patient is lying on a metal walkway on the surface of Mars with a fractured arm that is slowly losing circulation. But Laila had done her part. The arm was splinted, the pain was managed, the suit was maintaining pressure. Youssef was stable.

Stable, on Mars, was a word you used carefully.

"Youssef," Laila said, holding his right hand—his good hand—through the suit material. "How are you doing? Talk to me."

"Hurts," he said. The morphine was working but it was not erasing anything. The pain was still there, a thing he could feel at the edges of the medication, like a shoreline you could see through fog. "But I'm—Imani. Did you get clear?"

"I'm fine," Imani said. Her voice was tight. She was still kneeling beside him, her hands still supporting the splinted arm even though the splint was now holding it on its own. "I'm right here. I'm not moving. You're going to be fine, Youssef."

He smiled. It was a weak smile, a smile that cost him something to produce, but it was genuine. "You know what's funny," he said, and his voice was getting slurred by the medication and something else, something that was not fatigue but the body's way of saying it had reached a limit and was starting to shut things down to preserve the core. "What's funny is—it's just a panel. It's just a bolt. It's a maintenance check. The kind of thing I do every month."

"I know," Imani said.

"It's not dramatic," Youssef said. And there it was—not a lament, not a complaint, an observation. An observation about the nature of accidents, about the specific insult of an injury that is not earned in some grand way. Not heroic. Not tragic in the way tragedies are supposed to be in stories. Just the kind of thing that happened to mechanics, to workers, to people who turned bolts and tightened seals and ran their hands along panels looking for problems that they sometimes became. "It's the kind of thing that happens to mechanics everywhere. You know? It's not Mars-specific. It could've happened in a machine shop. In a garage. In a—" He stopped. "In a garage."

"Yeah," Imani said. She was crying. Not loudly. Quietly. The kind of crying you do when you are doing your job and your job does not permit you to stop and feel what you are feeling. "It could've happened anywhere."

"But we're on Mars," Youssef said. His eyes were closing now, not from sleep but from the medication and the pain and the body's understanding that consciousness was expensive and it could redirect that cost to more essential functions if it reduced awareness of things that could not be helped. "Everything's amplified. Every mistake. Every—every small thing. You don't get to be casual about anything. Not really."

"Save your energy," Laila said. Her voice was steady, but her eyes were on the splinted arm, on the color of the skin she could see through the suit's access port, on the subtle indicators of circulation that a physician learns to read the way a sailor reads the surface of the water. The color was not right. Not enough blood flow. The splint was holding the bone in place but it was not solving the vascular problem. The swelling was already compressing the brachial artery. She could feel it—in the pulse at his wrist, which was there but weaker than it should be, a thread of blood flow where there should have been a river.

*I have thirty seconds on the airlock cycle,* Mission AI said. *Laila, the patient's pulse in the injured arm is decreasing. Vascular compromise is progressing. You will need to address this in surgery."*

"I know," Laila said. She was looking at Youssef's face, at the way his breathing was slowing not from calm but from the medication's effect on his respiratory center, and she was calculating. Surgery would be required. Reduction of the fracture, possibly internal fixation if the bone could not be set manually, and vascular repair if the artery had been damaged by the displaced fragment. All of this was possible. The medical bay had the equipment for it. The issue was not capability. The issue was the chain of events between now and the operating table between now and Laila's hands inside the surgical bay.

Every link in that chain had to hold.

The airlock door opened. The corridor beyond it was warm and pressurized and lit by the soft light that the habitat systems provided as a poor substitute for sunlight. The transition from Mars to hab was always a shock—not a physical one but a psychological one, the sudden realization that you were no longer a visitor on an alien world but a resident in a human one. For a patient in pain, the shock was different. It was relief and it was terror at the same time, because relief meant the danger was past and terror meant the danger had entered a new phase where the outcomes were no longer in your hands.

Laila and Imani carried Youssef through the airlock together. It was not easy. The splint made the arm bulky, and every jolt of movement sent a signal through Youssef's nervous system that made his face tighten and his breath catch. But they did it the way you do everything on Mars: not efficiently, not gracefully, but deliberately, carefully, with enough attention to each step that nothing went wrong that did not need to go wrong.

They laid him on the medical bay's primary exam table. It was the first time in forty-seven minutes that Youssef had been horizontal without something underneath him being part of a machine or a vehicle or a surface that was not designed for human comfort. The table was soft—comparatively—and for a moment his face relaxed and Laila thought, with the specific tenderness that physicians carry for their patients in moments like this, *he looks so young.*

He was thirty-four. He was a structural engineer from Lagos, from a family that had wanted him to be a doctor, and he had chosen buildings instead because he liked the idea of making things that would outlast him. Now he was lying on an exam table on Mars with a broken arm, and the thing he had built—the thing he had worked on this morning, the panel that had been routine, the bolt that had been invisible—would outlast him in a way that he had never intended and that no one had wanted.

"Laila," he said. His voice was barely above a whisper, and the medication had pulled him to the edge of sleep where consciousness was a room whose door he could choose to open or close. "I'm going to be okay."

She put her hand on his forehead. Her fingers found his hair, which was close-cropped in a style that had not been fashionable in three months because barbers were not a priority on Mars. "I'm going to take care of you," she said. It was the thing physicians say to patients who need to believe it more than the physician does. "We're going to fix this."

He nodded. His eyes were closed. He was asleep, or something close to it—the morphine had pulled him down and his body had chosen to accept the invitation.

Laila turned to the surgical prep station and began to work. There was no drama in what she did. No urgency in the way urgency is portrayed in films. She washed her hands at the scrub sink, gloved, laid out her instruments, calibrated the imaging scanner that would show her the fracture pattern, and methodically prepared for a procedure she had done variations of a hundred times on Earth and zero times on Mars.

Zero times on Mars because on Mars the conditions were different. The gravity reduced the force required to manipulate the bone but also reduced the force available to stabilize it. The atmospheric pressure in the medical bay was 95 percent of Earth standard—not quite sea level—and the temperature was slightly cooler because the habitat's thermal budget had been optimized for power efficiency, not human comfort. These were small differences. In surgery, small differences were the category of difference that mattered most.

"Mission AI, bring up Youssef's left forearm radiograph."

The display above the exam table illuminated with the X-ray image Laila needed. It showed the fracture clearly: a comminuted fracture of the radius—the bone on the thumb side of the forearm—with a secondary fracture of the ulna, the companion bone. Both bones were broken. The fragments were displaced—the broken ends were not aligned, which meant that manual reduction was possible but would require precision and force and the kind of judgment that could not be delegated to anyone but the person standing at the table with their hands inside the surgical field.

"Comminuted fracture, radius and ulna," Laila said, speaking to Mission AI's log, to the record, to the documentation that would exist long after this moment had passed. "Displacement of approximately eighteen degrees. Vascular compromise in the brachial artery secondary to compression by displaced fragment. Patient is under general sedation. Beginning open reduction and internal fixation."

She made the incision. The skin opened. The tissue layers parted. She worked through the fascia, through the muscle, through the membranes that separated the blood vessels from the bone, and she found the fracture site the way a person finds a room in a house they grew up in—by a kind of knowing that is not visual but spatial, not observed but felt.

The bone was broken badly. She could see the fragments—three of them, not two, which meant the force of the impact had been greater than she had estimated. The largest fragment had shifted downward and medially, putting pressure on the brachial artery. The artery was intact but compressed. She could see the pulse in it—or rather, the absence of a strong pulse, the reduced flow, the diminished color of the tissue downstream.

"Clamp," she said, and the hand that offered her the instrument was steady because it had been trained to be steady, even when the person attached to it was not.

She manipulated the bone fragments with a surgeon's hands. These hands had performed this kind of procedure many times on Earth, in operating rooms with teams of assistants and full anesthesia support and the kind of institutional backing that made surgery a collaborative enterprise. On Mars, she was alone. There was no team. There was Mission AI in her ear, offering anatomical reference points and reminding her of procedures and monitoring Youssef's vital signs in real-time. There was Elena, standing outside the surgical bay, visible through the glass, not because she was needed but because she was the commander and a commander does not ask other people to carry a weight she would not stand beside.

Laila aligned the first fragment. Reduced it. Held it in place with a wire. Then the second fragment. Then the third. The process was methodical and slow and required the kind of patience that surgeons spend their entire careers building—the patience of a person whose instrument moves in millimeters and whose errors are measured the same way.

"Plate," she said.

The titanium plate was placed across the fracture, spanning the break, providing structural support where the bone's own structure had failed. Screws were inserted—six of them, three on each side of the fracture, each one driven into healthy bone to anchor the plate in a position that would allow the fracture to heal.

The procedure took two hours and eighteen minutes. When Laila finished, her hands were shaking—not from the surgery itself, but from the adrenaline crash, the way the body releases its emergency chemicals when the emergency is past and the person who held them is left with nothing but fatigue and the knowledge that there was nothing else to do right now.

She stepped back from the table and looked at Youssef. He was still sedated, still breathing still, his vital signs stable, the radiograph showing a clean reduction with the plate holding the fragments in the correct alignment. The surgery had been successful. The arm would heal. The bone would knit. In three months, six months, he would have a functioning left arm again.

Mission AI announced his vital signs. Heart rate: 72 beats per minute. Blood pressure: 118 over 74. Blood oxygen: 98 percent. All nominal. All within the range of a person recovering from a procedure under sedation. All telling Laila that the physical part of this—the part she could fix, the part that was in her domain, the part that responded to skill and instruments and the careful application of human knowledge to a physical problem—was handled.

She looked at Elena through the glass. Elena nodded once. It was not a nod of relief, exactly. It was a nod of acknowledgment: the physical problem had been addressed. The other problems remained.

Laila sat down on the stool beside the exam table, removed her gloves, and stared at Youssef's face for a long time. He was breathing rhythmically now. The sedation would last for another four hours, which was appropriate, which was what his body needed to begin the healing process. But healing was not the problem. Healing would happen. Bone was a tissue that understood how to repair itself. It did not need Laila's permission or her instructions. It needed time.

The problem was the other kind of healing. The kind that happened in the spaces between what could be fixed and what could not.

The accident report was sitting on Elena's desk when she returned to the command center. Mission AI had compiled it automatically—every data point, every timestamp, every sensor reading from Youssef's suit, the gangway, the thermal regulation array, and the bolt itself, which had been recovered by Imani after the medical evacuation and placed in a sealed container for analysis.

Elena sat at her desk and read the report the way she read everything: deliberately, from beginning to end, without skipping, because the details were where the truth lived. People wanted truth to be simple. They wanted it to arrive as a conclusion, a verdict, a label they could attach to an event and then move on from. But truth on Mars was never simple. Truth was a collection of details that could be arranged in different patterns, and the pattern you chose determined what you learned and what you missed.

*Mission AI: "Post-incident analysis, Day 437, 14:22 Station Time. Event: EVA crew injury during scheduled maintenance on Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Injury type: comminuted fracture, left forearm, radius and ulna, caused by panel displacement following bolt shear. Injured crew member: Youssef Diallo. Surgery completed successfully. Patient stable and sedated."*

*Root cause: bolt failure due to microfracture in bolt shaft. Analysis of recovered bolt fragment reveals a pre-existing stress crack—manufacturing defect, not wear-related. The crack is consistent with a flaw introduced during the bolt's initial production on Earth. Specifically: a hairline fracture approximately 2.3 millimeters in length, located at the thread root of the fastener, below the visual inspection threshold. The crack propagated under cyclic loading over the course of the mission's 437 days. Mars's temperature cycles—approximately 90 degrees Celsius between night minimum and day maximum in the Sector 7 location—created thermal stress that alternately opened and closed the crack, causing progressive growth. After 437 days and approximately 870 thermal cycles, the crack had grown to a critical length at which the remaining cross-section of the bolt could no longer sustain the applied load. Bolt 14 sheared."*

Elena read the analysis twice. She read it not because it was unclear—it was exceptionally clear, written with the precision of a document that knew the cost of every ambiguous word—but because she was looking for something. Not malice. Not negligence. Not human error. She was looking for the thing that would explain why a man she had trusted to go outside, to do a job he had done before, had come back broken.

And the explanation was worse than malice.

Malice you could punish. Malice you could identify, isolate, and prevent from happening again. Negligence you could correct with training, with procedure, with consequences. Human error you could design against with checklists, with redundancies, with the kind of systems thinking that turned mistakes into near-misses and near-misses into lessons.

But a manufacturing defect from Earth—a bolt made by a machine in a factory in a country on a continent that no one on Mars had thought about since loading, checked by a quality control process that had found nothing wrong because the crack was too small to find, shipped across three million kilometers of space, installed by a competent professional doing his job, and allowed to fail by the slow, patient physics of thermal cycling that no one had thought to model because it was just a bolt and bolts do not fail and bolts are part of the routine and routine is the word you use when you stop thinking about what a thing is made of and start only thinking about what a thing is for.

There was no villain. That was the worst thing about it. There was no villain, no incompetence, no corner cut, no procedure skipped. There was a bolt. A bolt made on Earth with a microscopic flaw. A bolt that did what bolts do under stress. A bolt that failed at the worst possible moment, when a person's arm was in the path of a releasing panel, and that arm was broken not because anyone did something wrong but because someone, somewhere, years ago, made a bolt that was almost right and almost right is the same as wrong on Mars.

Elena closed the report. She sat at her desk in the quiet of the command center—the lights were low, because it was afternoon and the crew was on their normal rotation, going about the tasks that continued even when one of them was injured—and she did what commanders do when the facts have been assembled and the analysis has been completed and the truth has been delivered in the most clinical terms available.

She let herself feel it.

Not for long. Not in a way that affected her judgment. But long enough to acknowledge the weight of what had just happened: a routine job, the kind of job done a thousand times a day by mechanics and engineers and workers on every planet and moon and space station humanity had ever reached, had gone wrong. And it had gone wrong not because of drama or conspiracy or the failure of any system that could be redesigned or any person who could be retrained. It had gone wrong because Mars amplifies everything. Every small thing. Every invisible thing. Every hairline crack in every bolt.

On Earth, that bolt would have been replaced during a standard maintenance interval, or it would have failed at some point during a building's life and been noticed during an inspection, or it would have failed and someone would have been mildly inconvenienced and replaced it and moved on. On Earth, a bolt failure is a nuisance.

On Mars, a bolt failure is a near-fatal injury.

The difference is not the bolt. The difference is the planet. The difference is the distance to the nearest hospital and the absence of the supply chain that makes Earth's tolerance for small failures possible. On Mars, there is no supply chain. There is no hardware store. There is no calling someone to bring a replacement. There is the bolt you have, and if the bolt you have is wrong, you do not get a second bolt until the next resupply mission, and the next resupply mission is a concept that no longer has a timeline.

Every task on Mars carries amplified risk. Not because the tasks are inherently dangerous—most of them are mundane, ordinary, the kind of work that goes unnoticed in industrial settings on Earth—but because Mars does not forgive the small failures that Earth's infrastructure absorbs. Earth is padded. Earth has redundancy built into every layer of its existence. Mars has thirty people and the machines they can fix and the air they can make. The padding is gone. The redundancy is limited. The margin between routine and emergency is the width of a hairline crack in a bolt.

Elena stood. She walked to the window that looked out over the habitat's exterior, over the gangway where Youssef had fallen, over the thermal regulation array where the panel sat now bolted back in place with a new fastener—a fastener that Imani had retrieved from Jonah's fabrication bay, a fastener that had been carefully inspected, measured, and cleared for use because this time everyone would check. Not because checking would guarantee safety—nothing guaranteed safety on Mars—but because checking was the only thing you could do besides stopping, and stopping was not an option for a species that had crossed three million kilometers to reach a world that did not want them.

She looked at the bolt. She could not see it from this distance, but she knew where it was. She knew that somewhere on that panel, in a row of sixteen identical fasteners, was one that had not been inspected with the kind of scrutiny that would have found a microfracture.    161|Imani turned to Youssef. "What are you feeling below the arm? In your hand? Your fingers?"
   162|
   163|"Sharp," he said. His voice was strained now, tight at the edges. "Like—like a hot wire. In the muscle. And dull—duller—at the bone itself. The dull part is worse. The sharp part moves when I move my fingers."

   167|"Yes. Shoulder is fine. It's between the elbow and the shoulder that—" He stopped, and his breathing got worse. "Imani. I'm getting dizzy."
   168|
   169|*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is one hundred and thirty-four beats per minute. Blood oxygen saturation is ninety-six percent, trending downward.    170|
   171|"I'm on it," Laila said. Her voice was close now—she had reached the outer airlock and was cycling through the first chamber. "Imani, do you have the auto-injector in the kit?"
   172|
   173|"Checking." Imani's gloved fingers moved through the med kit's organized compartments.    175|"Hold. Let me get eyes on him first. If I misdiagnose the type of fracture and the auto-injector masks the symptoms, I could miss a vascular compromise. But if he's going into shock from pain, I need to act fast. Youssef, stay with me. Keep talking to Imani."
   176|
   177|Youssef's hand found the grating of the walkway. His fingers curled, gripping the metal, and he was not gripping because he needed to hold on—he was gripping because gripping was something he could control. Control was the opposite of falling. Control was the opposite of the arm that had been perfectly fine one second and broken the next. Control was the thing he had clung to for four hundred and thirty-seven days on this planet and he was not going to let go of it now.
   178|
   179|The outer airlock opened. Laila emerged in her field suit—not a full EVA suit, but a lighter pressurized garment designed for corridor-to-airlock transitions, enough to protect her while the airlock cycled and fast enough to put on in thirty seconds. She reached Youssef in forty.
   180|
   181|Her first act was not medical. It was human. She put her hand on his shoulder—her actual hand, through the lightweight suit glove—and looked at his face through his visor and she did not smile and she did not look frightened.    182|
   183|"Youssef," she said. "I'm here. I'm going to take a look."
   184|
   185|She worked the service port open with practiced efficiency.    186|
   187|What she saw made her close her eyes for one-tenth of a second. One-tenth of a second was all she allowed herself.
   188|
   189|The arm inside the suit was at an angle that an arm should not be at. The bone was wrong. Not just broken—displaced.    190|
   191|"Vascular compromise imminent," Laila said quietly, speaking for Mission AI's log as much as for herself. "Displaced fracture, left forearm. Swelling is rapid.    192|
   193|"Do it," Youssef said. His jaw was tight. His face was pale even through the suit's lighting. "Do it now."
   194|
   195|Laila reached for the auto-injector. Morphine-analogue, 10 milligrams, designed for EVA use. She placed the injector against Youssef's neck through the suit's access port—where the suit was thinnest, where a puncture would not compromise integrity—and pressed the release.

   197|The medication worked fast. Not instantly—nothing biological worked instantly—but within thirty seconds Youssef's breathing was shallower but less ragged, his grip on the grating was looser, and his face had lost some of its tightness.

   199|"Better?" Laila asked.
   200|
   201|"Better," he said. The word was slurred. The medication was doing its job and the relief on his face was visible even through the visor.
   202|
   203|"Good. Now I'm going to open the sleeve section. Local decompression. Imani, be ready to support his arm when I release the pressure. The bone is going to shift when the suit tension is gone. We need to catch it in as neutral a position as possible."
   204|
   205|"Ready."

   207|Laila worked the sleeve's decompression valve. The suit's internal pressure in the left arm dropped from fifteen psi to eight. The sleeve went slack.    208|
   209|Youssef made a sound. It was not a scream. It was not a cry. It was the sound a person makes when their body tells them something that their mind already knew but had been hoping was wrong. A sound of confirmation, of a truth landing with finality.
   210|
   211|Imani's hands were there, gloved, supporting the arm, holding it in the most neutral position she could manage.    213|"Stable," Imani said. Her voice cracked on the word. She cleared it and said it again. "Stable. I've got it."

   217|"Mission AI, cycle the inner airlock. Emergency medical priority."
   218|
   219|*Inner airlock cycling. Estimated time to pressurized corridor access: three minutes, forty-five seconds. I have notified the medical bay of incoming patient. The surgical bay is being prepared. Tomas has been diverted from the fabrication bay and is heading to med. Elena is en route."*
   220|
   221|Three minutes and forty-five seconds.    222|
   223|Stable, on Mars, was a word you used carefully.
   224|
   225|"Youssef," Laila said, holding his right hand—his good hand—through the suit material. "How are you doing? Talk to me."
   226|
   227|"Hurts," he said. The morphine was working but it was not erasing anything. The pain was still there, a thing he could feel at the edges of the medication, like a shoreline you could see through fog. "But I'm—Imani. Did you get clear?"

   229|"I'm fine," Imani said. Her voice was tight. She was still kneeling beside him, her hands still supporting the splinted arm even though the splint was now holding it on its own. "I'm right here. I'm not moving. You're going to be fine, Youssef."
   230|
   231|He smiled. It was a weak smile, a smile that cost him something to produce, but it was genuine.    232|
   233|"I know," Imani said.
   234|
   235|"It's not dramatic," Youssef said. And there it was—not a lament, not a complaint, an observation.    237|"Yeah," Imani said. She was crying. Not loudly. Quietly. The kind of crying you do when you are doing your job and your job does not permit you to stop and feel what you are feeling. "It could've happened anywhere."
   238|
   239|"But we're on Mars," Youssef said.    240|
   241|"Save your energy," Laila said.    246|
   247|Every link in that chain had to hold.
   248|

   252|

   255|He was thirty-four.    300|
   301|The accident report was sitting on Elena's desk when she returned to the command center.    304|
   305|*Mission AI: "Post-incident analysis, Day 437, 14:22 Station Time. Event: EVA crew injury during scheduled maintenance on Sector 7 thermal regulation array.    307|*Root cause: bolt failure due to microfracture in bolt shaft. Analysis of recovered bolt fragment reveals a pre-existing stress crack—manufacturing defect, not wear-related.    309|Elena read the analysis twice.    310|
   311|And the explanation was worse than malice.
   312|
   313|Malice you could punish. Malice you could identify, isolate, and prevent from happening again. Negligence you could correct with training, with procedure, with consequences.    314|
   315|But a manufacturing defect from Earth—a bolt made by a machine in a factory in a country on a continent that no one on Mars had thought about since loading, checked by a quality control process that had found nothing wrong because the crack was too small to find, shipped across three million kilometers of space, installed by a competent professional doing his job, and allowed to fail by the slow, patient physics of thermal cycling that no one had thought to model because it was just a bolt and bolts do not fail and bolts are part of the routine and routine is the word you use when you stop thinking about what a thing is made of and start only thinking about what a thing is for.
   316|
   317|There was no villain. That was the worst thing about it. There was no villain, no incompetence, no corner cut, no procedure skipped. There was a bolt.    324|
   325|On Earth, that bolt would have been replaced during a standard maintenance interval, or it would have failed at some point during a building's life and been noticed during an inspection, or it would have failed and someone would have been mildly inconvenienced and replaced it and moved on. On Earth, a bolt failure is a nuisance.
   326|
   327|On Mars, a bolt failure is a near-fatal injury.
   328|
   329|The difference is not the bolt. The difference is the planet. There is no hardware store. There is no calling someone to bring a replacement.
