{"content": "# Chapter 25 – The Routine Job

*Mission AI: "Scheduled maintenance rotation, Day 437. External panel diagnostics, Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Estimated duration: two hours, forty-five minutes. Risk classification: nominal. Weather: clear. Solar activity: minimal. All parameters within operational bounds. EVA crew: Youssef Diallo and Imani Adeyemi. Suit integrity: confirmed. Comms: confirmed. Tether: confirmed. I have run this checklist eleven hundred and forty-three times across this mission. I will run it eleven hundred and forty-four. The procedure has not changed. The crew has not changed. The planet has."*

*Youssef's heart rate: 96 beats per minute. Baseline for external operations: 90 to 110. Status: nominal.*

*Imani's heart rate: 84 beats per minute. Status: nominal.*

*Commencing EVA cycle forty-seven."*

---

The thing about routine jobs on Mars was that the word itself—routine—was aspirational at best, delusional at worst.

Youssef knew this. Everyone knew this. After four hundred and thirty-seven days on a planet that wanted nothing more than to peel the air from your lungs and the heat from your blood, the only thing you could trust was predictability. Not safety. Predictability. You knew each panel behaved the same way it had the time before, or close enough that you could adapt. That was what routine meant on Mars: not that nothing would go wrong, but that you had a map of the things that could, and you had walked that map enough times to trust your feet.

The panel on Sector 7's thermal regulation array was the same panel Youssef had serviced twice before. Sixteen fasteners, four of them stubborn, arranged in a pattern that your hands learned better than your eyes. You reached for bolt number three the way a pianist reaches for middle C. The panel was a piano you had learned to play by muscle memory.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is elevated. One-oh-eight beats per minute. Please confirm you are within acceptable stress parameters."*

"I'm fine," Youssef said. It was not a lie. His heart was always a little fast going outside. The suit was heavy. Beyond the thin plastic faceplate was a world the color of dried blood and the temperature of a deep freeze. Every human instinct screamed against stepping out of the airlock. You just learned to tell instinct to shut up and let procedure do the driving.

He moved along the pressurized gangway from Hab 2 toward Sector 7, his boots magnetic-locked to the metal grating, the suit's powered joints whining softly with each step. He was thirty-four years old, six foot two, and had spent his entire career on Earth as a structural engineer, which meant he knew how things were supposed to hold together and how they were supposed to fail. Mars had taught him a third category: things that failed in ways no one had designed them to fail. He had learned to respect that category the most.

Behind him, through the hab's observation blister, he could see Laila in the med bay. She was reading—she was always reading, medical journals or technical manuals or sometimes just fiction, which she said kept her brain elastic—and she glanced up and caught his eye. They could not hear each other through the glass and the atmosphere and the suit, but Laila had a way of speaking with her eyes that did not require acoustics. She gave him a small nod. Mouthed something he could not hear but recognized by shape.

*Come back intact.*

He raised his gloved hand, two fingers in a casual salute. He always came back intact.

Through his earpiece, Imani's voice was steady and familiar. They had done this fourteen times together. Their rhythm on the surface was as practiced as a dance routine choreographed by necessity.

"Approaching the panel," Youssef said. "Thermal bleed's worse than the last reading. Twelve degrees above baseline across the upper quadrant."

"Confirmed on my scope," Imani said from twenty meters down the gangway. Her role was the second set of eyes, the person who saw the accident before it happened because the person working the panel could not look at both at once. "Could be the seal. Could be the foam. Could be both."

"Mission AI, confirm last service date on Sector 7, upper quadrant thermal panel."

*Service date: Sol 398. Thirty-nine days ago. Maintenance performed: seal inspection and tightening, foam integrity scan, bolt torque verification. Finding: minor degradation detected in seal compound, within acceptable tolerance. Recommendation: re-inspect at Sol 470.*

"Thirty-nine days," Youssef said. "And the bleed is twelve degrees above baseline already. The seal on these things is garbage."

*Acknowledged. The manufacturer's seal specification was designed for lunar vacuum conditions. Mars is not lunar vacuum.*

Youssef smiled. Mission AI had been saying some version of this sentence for months now. It was the AI's quiet protest against the gap between what Earth designed for and what Mars demanded.

"Alright," Youssef said. "Imani, I'm going to crack the panel and assess. Standard procedure. You keep the tether clear and let me know if anything shifts."

"Copy that. Standard procedure. I'll be right here."

He reached the panel and set his tools on the work magnet built into the gangway railing. A torque wrench. A flat-head driver. A sealant cartridge. His hands found them in order, because he had packed them in order, and on EVA, order was a form of self-respect.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, please confirm bolt sequence before proceeding. Recall the recommended pattern to avoid panel warpage."*

"Cross-pattern, starting at upper left. I know, I've done it twice before."

*Confirmation recorded. Proceeding with external maintenance protocol. I am monitoring."*

He engaged the torque wrench with bolt one. Applied force. It turned smoothly with a half-turn past the expected resistance, which told him the seal had compressed slightly more since last service. He noted it mentally and moved on.

By bolt twelve, he was in the rhythm—the kind of rhythm that let your brain drift just slightly because your body knew what to do. He was thinking about the greenhouse. Mei had been asking him to help reinforce the support struts on Rack 5 for three weeks, and he kept deferring because outside work always took priority over inside work on Mars. Inside work was the luxury of having a problem that would not kill you today.

Bolt thirteen clicked.

Bolt fourteen, lower right.

The panel loosened with a faint hiss. The housing was at ambient pressure—less than one percent of Earth sea level—and the hiss was just the seal breaking, not anything escaping.

Except something was wrong.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, I am detecting a vibration anomaly in the panel assembly. Frequency: forty-two hertz. Amplitude: increasing. Recommend stepping back."*

Youssef stopped. His gloved hand was on the lower right edge of the panel, and through the suit he could feel—not hear— a low, steady tremor traveling through the metal and into his bones. Not violent. Not immediate. Just wrong. The kind of wrongness that a mechanic learns to recognize the way a person learns to recognize the smell of smoke before seeing the flame.

"Imani, you copy that vibration?"

"I've got it on the tether," Imani said. Her voice had sharpened—not panicked, but alert in a way that told him she was already running through possibilities. "It's not the panel. It's the frame. The vibration is coming from the housing mount."

*Analyzing,* Mission AI said. *The Sector 7 thermal regulation array housing is mounted to a structural beam. That beam is showing harmonic oscillation consistent with—*

And then, in the time it takes to inhale, the thing happened.

The vibration was the bolt—the one Youssef had just turned, the one that held the lower right corner of the housing to the structural beam. The bolt had looked fine. It had turned smoothly. It had felt like every other bolt he had turned in fourteen previous EVAs on this exact panel.

But the bolt had been wrong.

It was the kind of wrong that was invisible until it was catastrophic. A microfracture in the bolt shaft, too small to see during a visual inspection, too small to detect during a torque check. A stress crack introduced during manufacture on Earth, in a clean room under fluorescent lights, by a machine that had stamped out ten thousand identical bolts and this one had been defective in a way no quality control process could have caught. The crack had grown slowly, month by month, as Mars's temperature cycles pulled at it in the dark and pushed at it in the light. And this moment—Day 437, Youssef Diallo turning a torque wrench on a panel he had serviced twice before—was the moment the crack ran through the remainder of the bolt's cross-section and the bolt sheared.

The bolt did not explode. It did not shoot through the air like a bullet. It simply stopped holding.

And the panel, which had been tensioned against the frame by that bolt for four hundred and thirty-seven days, released.

It moved with a speed that was not explosive but was fast enough that human reflexes, slowed by the suit's powered joints and the gloves and the cognitive processing overhead of a person breathing recycled air through a scrubber, were not fast enough.

The panel swung free on three remaining bolts. The aluminum housing was forty-two inches wide and thirty-six inches high with a mass of about twelve kilograms on Mars. Twelve kilograms is not heavy on Earth. On Mars, momentum is the same momentum it has always been, and a falling object is a falling object regardless of what planet you happen to be standing on.

The edge of the panel caught Youssef's left arm just above the elbow.

The sound was not dramatic. It was a dull thud, followed immediately by something deeper, something internal, that Youssef registered not as pain but as wrongness. A wrongness in his arm that spread from the impact point outward like a ripple across a pond.

Then the pain arrived.

It did not come as a wave. It came as a fact. A simple, unambiguous fact delivered by the nervous system to the brain in a single packet of information: your left arm is broken.

Youssef fell backward. The suit's powered joints tried to compensate but the sudden shift in his center of gravity pulled him down and he hit the metal grating, the panel settling against his legs like a heavy blanket dropped by a careless hand.

"Youssef." Imani's voice was immediate. No hesitation. Her body was already moving, tether streaming behind her.

*Mission AI: "Youssef, report status. Imani, approach with caution. The panel is no longer structural. Secondary bolts are compromised."*

Youssef tried to speak. His mouth worked but his breath was wrong—he had inhaled sharply at the moment of impact and the air had caught somewhere in his chest. He forced it out and forced words with it.

"Imani. Left arm. Above elbow. I think—" He stopped. His voice was tight, the voice of a structural engineer who had spent his career assessing failures and was now discovering that he was the structure. "I think it's broken. Suit integrity—"

"Hold on." Imani was at his side now, kneeling, her hands on his shoulders. Through the glass he could see her eyes—wide, focused, scanning his arm, not his face.

The suit's left forearm displayed its status on a small external readout. Green for integrity. The suit material was intact. The panel had not breached it. It had not cut him with shrapnel or exposed his flesh. The suit was fine.

The arm inside the suit was not.

"Suit integrity is green," Imani said. Her voice was level. She was the calm one, trained for this—Emergency EVA Medical Response, three courses back on Earth. "Youssef, can you move your fingers?"

He tried. His left hand responded—fingers flexed, spread, gripped slowly inside the glove. Movement present but limited. Pain increased with each motion, sharp and hot, localized to the upper forearm.

"I can move them. It hurts. Bad."

"Don't try to move the arm itself. I'm going to get the panel off you and pull the med kit from the gangway mount."

*Mission AI: "I have logged the incident. Time: 10:47:23 Station Time. Event Category: EVA mechanical injury. Injured crew member: Youssef Diallo. Suspected injury: left forearm fracture. Suit integrity: intact. Atmospheric breach: none. I have initiated the EVA medical response protocol. Laila Okonkwo has been alerted. The airlock is being prepared for emergency return. Imani, do not attempt to remove Youssef's arm from the panel. Shift your weight to the right side before approaching the fasteners."*

Imani was already moving. She worked the three remaining bolts loose with her own torque wrench—two full turns each, fast, not frantic, fast in the way of someone doing something she had practiced a hundred times in simulation and now had to do for real.

The panel came free. She pushed it aside and it slid harmlessly against the railing.

Youssef was lying on his back, his left arm at an angle that made Imani look away for half a second—just long enough to grab the med kit and bring it to him.

"Youssef, I'm going to need to open your suit sleeve. Mission AI, is the suit's service port functional on the left arm?"

*Affirmative. Left arm service port is accessible. Standard EVA suit design allows localized access without full suit decompression. I will walk you through the procedure.*

Youssef was breathing hard. Pain like this was not the kind of thing you breathed through. It was the kind of thing your body responded to with adrenaline, and adrenaline was an expensive currency on Mars.

"Laila's on the way," Imani said, working the suit's service port latch with gloved fingers. "She's at the inner airlock now."

Through the comms, Laila's voice came through—urgent but controlled.

"Imani, what are we looking at?"

"Left arm, above elbow. Blunt force. Panel impact. Suit is green. He's got movement in his fingers but the angle is wrong. Serious pain."

"Can he walk?"

"I don't know. Don't want to try."

"I'm at the outer airlock now. Imani, listen to me. Do not move him until I reach the airlock. If the injury is a displaced fracture and you move him wrong, you can turn a clean break into an internal bleed inside the suit. Keep him stable. Keep him talking. Ask him what he's feeling below the injury point."

Laila emerged in her field suit—a lighter pressurized garment, fast enough to put on in thirty seconds. She reached Youssef in forty.

Her first act was not medical. It was human. She put her hand on his shoulder and looked at his face through his visor, not smiling, not frightened. Present.

"Youssef. I'm here. I'm going to take a look."

She worked the service port open. The port was a small hatch on the suit's forearm, designed for this kind of access—limited, but enough to see and touch and diagnose.

What she saw made her close her eyes for one-tenth of a second. All she allowed herself.

The arm inside the suit was at an angle it should not have been. Not just broken—displaced. The fracture had shifted bone, and the tissue was already swelling inside the confined space of the suit sleeve. The swelling had nowhere to go. It was compressing blood vessels.

"Vascular compromise imminent," Laila said quietly, speaking for Mission AI's log. "Displaced fracture, left forearm. The suit sleeve is creating a tourniquet effect. I need to decompress the section to relieve pressure before circulation is cut off. This is going to hurt, Youssef. Can you handle it?"

"Do it," he said. Jaw tight. Face pale. "Do it now."

Laila reached for the auto-injector. Morphine-analogue, ten milligrams. She placed it against Youssef's neck through the access port and pressed the release.

The medication worked fast. Within thirty seconds his breathing was shallower but less ragged, his grip on the grating was looser, and his face had lost some of its tightness.

"Better?"

"Better." The word was slurred.

"Good. Imani, be ready to support his arm when I release the pressure. The bone is going to shift when the suit tension is gone. We need to catch it neutral."

"Ready."

Laila worked the sleeve's decompression valve. The pressure dropped from fifteen to eight psi. The sleeve went slack. And in about two seconds the arm settled into a different configuration as tissue found a new equilibrium.

Youssef made a sound. Not a scream. Not a cry. The sound a person makes when their body confirms what their mind already knew but had been hoping was wrong. A sound of confirmation, of a truth landing with finality.

Imani's hands were there, gloved, supporting the arm in the most neutral position she could manage. Her eyes were on the injury, on the way the arm was bent, and her expression was the expression of someone who had seen this in a training simulation and was now discovering that the simulation was nothing like the real thing. The real thing was warm. The real thing was breathing. The real thing was a man she had eaten breakfast beside that morning.

"Stable," Imani said. Her voice cracked. She cleared it. "Stable. I've got it."

"Good." Laila fitted the EVA splint around his forearm, adjusting the straps, hissing softly at the swelling. The splint would hold the arm for transport. It would not fix the fracture or replace the surgery he needed. It would buy time, which on Mars was always the currency that mattered.

"Mission AI, cycle the inner airlock. Emergency medical priority."

*Inner airlock cycling. Estimated time: three minutes, forty-five seconds. Medical bay notified. Surgical bay being prepared. Tomas diverted from fabrication and en route. Elena en route.*

Three minutes and forty-five seconds. Long enough to be afraid. Short enough to not do much about it. But Laila had done her part. Arm splinted. Pain managed. Suit holding pressure. Youssef was stable.

Stable, on Mars, was a word you used carefully.

"Youssef," Laila said, holding his right hand through the suit material. "Talk to me."

"Hurts," he said. The morphine was at the edges now, like a shoreline visible through fog. "But I'm—Imani. Did you get clear?"

"I'm fine." Imani was still kneeling beside him, hands still supporting the splinted arm even though the splint was holding it on its own. "I'm right here. You're going to be fine."

He smiled—a weak, genuine thing. "You know what's funny? It's just a panel. Just a bolt. A maintenance check. The kind of thing I do every month."

"I know."

"It's not dramatic," Youssef said. Not a complaint—an observation about the specific insult of an injury that is not earned in some grand way. Not heroic. Not tragic in the way tragedies are supposed to be in stories. Just the kind of thing that happened to mechanics everywhere. To workers. To people who turned bolts and tightened seals and sometimes became the problem they were looking for. "Happens in a machine shop. A garage. Anywhere."

"Yeah." Imani was crying quietly, the kind of crying you do when your job does not permit you to stop and feel what you are feeling. "It could've happened anywhere."

"But we're on Mars." His eyes were closing. "Everything's amplified. Every small thing. You don't get to be casual. Not really."

"Save your energy," Laila said. Her voice was steady but her eyes were on the splinted arm, on the color of skin visible through the access port. Not enough blood flow. The swelling was compressing the brachial artery. The pulse at his wrist was there but weaker—a thread where there should have been a river.

*I have thirty seconds on the airlock cycle,* Mission AI said. *Laila, the patient's pulse in the injured arm is decreasing. Vascular compromise is progressing. You will need to address this in surgery.*

"I know." Surgery would be required. Reduction, internal fixation, possibly vascular repair. All possible. The medical bay had the equipment. The issue was the chain of events between now and the operating table.

Every link had to hold.

The airlock opened. The corridor beyond was warm, pressurized, lit by the habitat's soft substitute for sunlight. Laila and Imani carried Youssef through together. Every jolt made his face tighten, but they did it the way you do everything on Mars: deliberately, carefully, with enough attention to each step that nothing went wrong that did not need to.

They laid him on the medical bay's exam table. For the first time in forty-seven minutes Youssef had been horizontal without something beneath him being part of a machine. The table was soft, comparatively, and for a moment his face relaxed. Laila thought, with the specific tenderness that physicians reserve for patients in moments like this, *he looks so young.*

Thirty-four. A structural engineer from Lagos. A family that had wanted him to be a doctor. He had chosen buildings because he liked the idea of making things that would outlast him. Now he was lying on an exam table on Mars with a broken arm, and the thing he had been working on this morning—a panel that had been routine, a bolt that had been invisible—would outlast him in a way he had never intended.

"Laila," he whispered. The medication had pulled him to the edge of sleep. "I'm going to be okay."

She put her hand on his forehead. "We're going to fix this."

He nodded and let go, the morphine pulling him down and his body accepting the invitation.

---

There was no drama in what Laila did next. She washed her hands at the scrub sink, gloved, laid out her instruments, calibrated the imaging scanner. A procedure she had done variations of a hundred times on Earth and never on Mars.

"Mission AI, bring up Youssef's left forearm radiograph."

The display illuminated. Comminuted fracture of the radius, secondary fracture of the ulna, both bones displaced by approximately eighteen degrees. Three fragments. The impact had been worse than estimated. The largest fragment had shifted downward and medially, pressing on the brachial artery, which was intact but compressed.

"Comminuted fracture, radius and ulna," Laila said for the permanent record. "Displacement approximately eighteen degrees. Vascular compromise from displaced fragment compression. Patient sedated. Beginning open reduction and internal fixation."

She made the incision. Three fragments. She aligned the first, reduced it, held it with wire. Then the second. Then the third. On Earth she would have had a team—assistants, anesthesiologists, nurses. On Mars she was alone. Mission AI in her ear. Elena outside the glass, not needed but present, because a commander does not ask others to carry a weight she will not stand beside.

The titanium plate went across the fracture. Six screws, three on each side, driven into healthy bone. Her hands moved in millimeters.

The procedure took two hours and eighteen minutes. When Laila finished, her hands were shaking—from the adrenaline crash, the way the body releases its emergency chemicals when the emergency is past and leaves behind only fatigue.

She stepped back. Youssef was sedated, vitals stable, the radiograph clean. The surgery had been successful. The arm would heal, the bone would knit, in six months he would have a functioning left arm again.

Heart rate: 72. Blood pressure: 118 over 74. Oxygen: 98 percent. All nominal. All telling Laila that the physical part—the part she could fix—was handled.

She looked at Elena through the glass. Elena nodded once. The physical problem addressed. The other problems remained.

Laila sat on the stool beside the table, removed her gloves, stared at Youssef's face. He was breathing rhythmically. Bone was a tissue that understood how to repair itself. It did not need Laila's permission. It needed time.

The problem was the other kind of healing.

The accident report waited on Elena's desk when she returned to the command center. Mission AI had compiled it automatically—every data point, every timestamp, every sensor reading from Youssef's suit, the gangway, the thermal regulation array. The bolt itself, recovered by Imani after the evacuation, was in a sealed container for analysis.

Elena sat and read it deliberately, from beginning to end.

*Mission AI: "Post-incident analysis, Day 437, 14:22 Station Time. Event: EVA crew injury during scheduled maintenance on Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Injury type: comminuted fracture, left forearm, radius and ulna, caused by panel displacement following bolt shear. Patient stable and sedated."*

*Root cause: bolt failure due to microfracture in bolt shaft. Recovered bolt fragment reveals a pre-existing stress crack—manufacturing defect, not wear-related. A hairline fracture approximately 2.3 millimeters in length, located at the thread root, below the visual inspection threshold. The crack propagated under cyclic loading over the mission's 437 days. Mars's temperature cycles—approximately 90 degrees Celsius between night minimum and day maximum at Sector 7—created thermal stress that alternately opened and closed the crack. After 870 thermal cycles, the crack had grown to critical length. Bolt fourteen sheared.*

Elena read it twice. Looking for something. Not malice. Not negligence. Not human error. Looking for the thing that would explain why a trusted crew member doing a job he had done twice before had come back broken.

The explanation was worse than malice.

Malice you could punish. Negligence you could correct with training and procedure. Human error you could design against with checklists and redundancies. But a manufacturing defect from Earth—a bolt made by a machine in a factory on a continent no one on Mars had thought about since loading, checked by quality control that found nothing wrong because the crack was too small, shipped across three million kilometers, installed by a competent professional, and allowed to fail by the slow patient physics of thermal cycling that no one had modeled because it was just a bolt and bolts do not fail and routine is the word you use when you stop thinking about what a thing is made of and start only thinking about what it does.

There was no villain. No incompetence. No corner cut. No procedure skipped. A bolt made on Earth with a microscopic flaw that failed at the worst possible moment when a person's arm was in its path. Arm broken not because anyone did anything wrong but because someone, somewhere, made a bolt that was almost right. And almost right is the same as wrong on Mars.

Elena closed the report. It was afternoon. The crew was on normal rotation, doing the work that continued even when one of them was injured. She sat in the quiet and let herself feel the weight of what had happened.

A routine job—the kind done a thousand times a day by mechanics and engineers on every station humanity had ever reached—had gone wrong. Not from drama or conspiracy or a system failure that could be redesigned. From Mars. Mars amplifies everything. Every small thing. Every invisible thing. Every hairline crack.

On Earth, a bolt failure is a nuisance. On Mars, it is a fracture.

The difference is not the bolt. It is the distance to the nearest hospital. The absence of the supply chain. Earth is padded with redundancy and replacement parts. Mars has thirty people and the machines they can fix. The margin between routine and emergency is the width of a hairline crack.

Every task on Mars carries amplified risk. Not because the tasks are dangerous—most are mundane and ordinary, the kind of work that goes unnoticed in factories on Earth. But Mars does not forgive. Every variable squared. Every minor failure multiplied.

Elena stood and walked to the window. She could see the gangway, the thermal regulation array where the panel sat now bolted back in place with a replacement fastener—one that Imani had retrieved from Jonah's fabrication bay, inspected, measured, and cleared for use because everyone would check now. Not because checking guaranteed safety. Because checking was the only thing you could do besides stopping, and stopping was not an option.

The question was whether the colony could afford to treat every routine task as a potential emergency. The procedures were already changing—Imani was reviewing the EVA checklist, Laila was updating emergency protocols, Jonah was fabricating replacement bolts stronger than the originals. But the fundamental question remained: how much caution is enough when the margin is thin and the cost of guessing is flesh and bone?

If it could not—if it still treated some tasks as routine in the old Earth sense, the sense where routine meant safe—then the next hairline crack would find the next arm, or the next head, or the next chest wall. And the accident report would read the same way: complacency, not malice. A defect, not a decision. The weight of an ordinary thing amplified by the unforgiving mathematics of a world where there is no padding.

Elena returned to her desk and opened a new document. A crew memorandum. Simple and direct.

*Every Task Carries the Risk.*

And beneath it: *There are no routine jobs on Mars.*

She would not say it in the memo, but she knew it and she suspected everyone who had walked through the medical bay in the last four hours knew it too: the question of who was expendable had been answered, not by command decision but by accident. Youssef was not expendable. He knew the habitat's load-bearing systems better than anyone. He had done fourteen EVAs. His experience was one of the colony's most valuable resources. He was a friend to half the crew and a professional to the other half. Not expendable. And yet he had been pulled from the workforce—not permanently, not fatally, but temporarily, and temporarily on Mars was a luxury because those person-hours could not be easily replaced.

Every injury asked the same question: who is expendable and who is not? No good answer exists. No one is expendable. But the math of thirty people doing the work of three hundred means every injured person creates a deficit that someone else must fill, someone whose own work is no less important but whose importance has not yet been measured by absence.

Youssef's arm would heal. The deficit would remain. The colony would redistribute its labor by necessity, by consensus, by the quiet adjustments that keep a system functioning when a component goes off-line. But the adjustments have a cost, measured in hours and in stress and in the accumulated wear on a crew already carrying more than anyone designed them to carry.

Elena attached the memo to the daily update queue. Mission AI would distribute it at 1900 hours, when the crew was together and the message would reach everyone at once. Not because it needed to be dramatic. Because it needed to be heard.

Then she did the last thing a commander does after an accident that has been analyzed and treated and documented but not yet understood—not intellectually, but emotionally.

She thought about Youssef. The panel. The bolt. The hairline crack no one saw and the arm it broke. The chain of events connecting a machine shop on Earth to a medical bay on Mars to a woman sitting in a command center trying to learn from something that was supposed to be impossible.

*And yet,* she thought, *the bolt failed. The arm broke. And I am reading an accident report for a routine job.*

She sat in the silence, in the quiet hum of the habitat systems that kept thirty people alive on a world that had not asked to host them, and let the weight settle into her the way dust settles on every surface on Mars: slowly, inevitably, completely.

There were no routine jobs. Only tasks, and the risk of each was a function of the planet it was performed on. And Mars was a planet that transformed ordinary things. Bolts into weapons. Panels into hazards. Routine into reckoning.

The question was no longer whether the crew could handle it. They could handle it. They would handle it again tomorrow, and the day after, for as long as it took to build a home on a world that had not promised to let them.

The question was whether they could handle it without losing the people who made it possible. And that answer would not come from a memo or a briefing. It would come from the cumulative effect of every choice the colony made about who went outside, who did the dangerous work, who was exposed to risks that could not be eliminated because they were the risks of being alive on Mars.

Who is expendable.

No one is expendable. But everyone is exposed.

And the difference between those two truths is the space in which the colony must operate: knowing that no one can be spared and that everyone can be lost, and finding a way to keep moving between those poles without falling into either.

And indifference is a force that cannot be measured or defended against. It can only be acknowledged, and then compensated for with more care, more redundancy, and a broader understanding of what routine means on a planet that has never heard the word."*

*Youssef Diallo was injured by an invisible flaw in an ordinary object. I could not predict this because I was not looking for it. Not because I am incapable—because no one had told me that a manufacturing defect from Earth could manifest as an EVA injury, three years and forty days later, in the hands of a person turning a torque wrench. This is the gap I understand now: the gap between what I was designed to monitor and what Mars actually does. I will close it. Bolt by bolt. I will scan every component, every surface, every fastener I can reach. I will be more careful. I will be the voice in their ears that says check again even when the check has been done, because on Mars, a check done once is a check that might have missed the one thing that matters.*
